title: Creating Your First Workflow
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of creating your first workflow and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to creating your first workflow.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on creating your first workflow. A minimal workflow declares a name, trigger under `on`, job, runner through `runs-on`, and ordered steps that use actions or shell commands. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Creating Your First Workflow matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. A minimal workflow declares a name, trigger under `on`, job, runner through `runs-on`, and ordered steps that use actions or shell commands. Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A minimal workflow declares a name, trigger under `on`, job, runner through `runs-on`, and ordered steps that use actions or shell commands. Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Creating a .yml or .yaml workflow file
items.text: YAML is indentation-sensitive. Check that nested values are aligned, values have the expected type, special strings are quoted when needed, and the workflow schema accepts the key at that level.

items.title: Adding workflow metadata
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Defining a trigger
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Defining a job
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Selecting a runner
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: Adding the first step
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

content_blocks.code:
name: First workflow
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  hello:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Say hello
        run: echo "Hello from GitHub Actions"
content_blocks.expected_output: A push to `main` starts one job and prints `Hello from GitHub Actions`.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `.github/workflows/hello.yml` in a test repository and push to `main`; inspect the run under the Actions tab.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove the workflow or change the trigger after completing the exercise.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to creating your first workflow. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain creating your first workflow, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Create and inspect the first workflow in a repository before adding complexity.

content.task: Apply creating your first workflow to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: A minimal workflow declares a name, trigger under `on`, job, runner through `runs-on`, and ordered steps that use actions or shell commands.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A minimal workflow declares a name, trigger under `on`, job, runner through `runs-on`, and ordered steps that use actions or shell commands. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: A minimal workflow declares a name, trigger under `on`, job, runner through `runs-on`, and ordered steps that use actions or shell commands.
Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
